blocks.title: Interoperability Test Bed

# Interoperability Test Bed

![BuildStatus](https://github.com/ISAITB/gitb/actions/workflows/quality.yml/badge.svg)
[![Security Rating](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project=ISAITB_gitb&metric=security_rating)](https://sonarcloud.io/summary/new_code?id=ISAITB_gitb)
[![Maintainability Rating](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project=ISAITB_gitb&metric=sqale_rating)](https://sonarcloud.io/summary/new_code?id=ISAITB_gitb)
[![Reliability Rating](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project=ISAITB_gitb&metric=reliability_rating)](https://sonarcloud.io/

summary.text: Introduces the Interoperability Test Bed, a European Commission DIGIT service for conformance testing of IT systems through scenario-based test cases written in the GITB Test Description Language (TDL), whose steps use built-in capabilities or orchestrate extension services. Test cases typically exchange and validate messages with a system under test, and may include control flow, user interaction and data processing; the Test Bed also offers a user interface, a REST API and webhooks. DIGIT runs a shared instance and publishes all components as Docker images for local use. The section opens with build, quality, licence, documentation and Docker badges.

blocks.title: About this repository
blocks.content:
## About this repository

This repository contains the main application components that are used by the Interoperability Test Bed. These are:
- The **test engine**, responsible for executing test cases and reporting their progress and outcome.
  In terms of Docker images, this component represents the ``gitb-srv`` image.
- The **frontend**, responsible for the Test Bed's user interface and its test, user, and configuration
  management features. In terms of Docker images, this component represents the ``gitb-ui`` image.

In subsequent sections these components are referred to using their Docke

summary.text: Says the repository holds the Test Bed's two main application components: the test engine, which executes test cases and reports progress and outcome (Docker image gitb-srv), and the frontend, which provides the user interface and test, user and configuration management (gitb-ui). It notes that the simplest way to use the Test Bed is through the published Docker images and the installation guide, with building from source as the alternative.

Documentation highlights include:

summary.text: Points to the Test Bed's documentation hub on the Interoperable Europe Portal and lists highlights: the developer onboarding guide, the user guide, reference documentation for GITB TDL and GITB test services, and installation guides for development and production. Newcomers are advised to start with the onboarding guide and then follow tutorials on a first test case, simple messaging and complex testing.

blocks.title: Technology stack
blocks.content:
# Technology stack

Both ``gitb-srv`` and ``gitb-ui`` are Java-based applications. Specifically, ``gitb-srv`` is packaged
as a Spring Boot application using Akka as its primary internal framework, whereas ``gitb-ui``
is developed in Scala and uses the Play Framework.

The frontend of the ``gitb-ui`` component is an Angular app developed in TypeScript, and is managed in terms
of scaffolding and build using Angular CLI.

summary.text: States that gitb-srv and gitb-ui are both Java-based: gitb-srv is a Spring Boot application using Akka internally, gitb-ui is written in Scala on the Play Framework, and gitb-ui's frontend is an Angular TypeScript app built with Angular CLI.

blocks.title: Configuration properties
blocks.content:
# Configuration properties

The main configuration file of interest is ``application.conf`` from ``gitb-ui`` although this never needs
to be adapted directly. All properties can be set through environment variables, provided either via Docker
or through the IDE used for development.

The full listing and documentation of properties is available [here](https://www.itb.ec.europa.eu/docs/guides/latest/installingTheTestBedProduction/index.html#configuration-properties).

summary.text: Notes that the main configuration file is gitb-ui's application.conf, which never needs direct editing because every property can be set through environment variables, via Docker or the IDE; the full list of properties is documented in the production installation guide.

blocks.title: Build for development
blocks.content:
# Build for development

Follow these steps to build and run the application components for development purposes.

summary.text: Heading that introduces the steps to build and run the components for development; it carries no further content.

blocks.title: Prerequisites
blocks.content:
## Prerequisites

To build and run the Test Bed's components you need to have the following tools:
- JDK 21+, used as the base platform for both ``gitb-srv`` and ``gitb-ui``.
- Maven 3.9+, used to build ``gitb-srv``.
- SBT 1.10+, used to build ``gitb-ui``.
- Scala 2.13+, used to build the backend app of ``gitb-ui``.
- Node version 22+, used to build the frontend app of ``gitb-ui``.

Although not mandatory, the proposed IDE to use is IntelliJ, and VS Code for ``gitb-ui``'s Angular app.

summary.text: Lists the tools needed to build and run the components: JDK 21+, Maven 3.9+ (for gitb-srv), SBT 1.10+ and Scala 2.13+ (for gitb-ui's backend) and Node 22+ (for gitb-ui's frontend), with IntelliJ and VS Code suggested but not required.

blocks.title: Additional Test Bed components
blocks.content:
### Additional Test Bed components

The focus of this README file is the ``gitb-srv`` and ``gitb-ui`` components. To run a complete Test Bed instance
you will also require at least:
- A MySQL database (version 8+) for its persistence.
- A REDIS instance (version 7+) for the caching of user sessions.

Both these instances are set up separately (e.g. via Docker) environment. These can be set up from Docker
as follows:
- MySQL: ``docker run --name gitb-mysql -p 3306:3306 -d isaitb/gitb-mysql``
- REDIS: ``docker run --name gitb-redis -p 6379:6379 -d isaitb/gitb-redis``

> **Note**  
> 
> All image

summary.text: Notes that a complete Test Bed instance also needs a MySQL 8+ database for persistence and a Redis 7+ instance for session caching, both set up separately, and gives docker run commands for the isaitb/gitb-mysql and isaitb/gitb-redis images; all images are defined in docker-compose.yml.

blocks.title: Test engine (gitb-srv)
blocks.content:
## Test engine (gitb-srv)

To build and run the ``gitb-srv`` component carry out the following steps:
1. From folder ``gitb`` run ``mvn clean install -DskipTests=true``.
2. Create a run configuration in your IDE as follows (or set up outside your IDE). The run configuration
   can be defined in one of two ways:
   - **As a Java Application (best):** Set class ``Application`` from the ``gitb-testbed-service`` module as
     your entry point. This is the best approach as it allows direct debugging without extra configuration.
   - **Via Maven:** Run ``mvn spring-boot:run`` from the ``gitb-testbe

summary.text: Gives the development steps for gitb-srv: build with mvn clean install -DskipTests=true, run it either as a Java application with entry class Application in the gitb-testbed-service module (preferred, for direct debugging) or with mvn spring-boot:run, and set the environment variables remote.testcase.repository.url and remote.testresource.repository.url to the local gitb-ui repository endpoints on port 9000.

blocks.title: Frontend (gitb-ui)
blocks.content:
## Frontend (gitb-ui)

To build and run the ``gitb-ui`` component carry out the following steps:
1. From the ``gitb-ui`` folder issue ``sbt compile``.
2. Define in your IDE a run configuration as a sbt application to run ``sbt run``.
3. Set environment variables as needed. For example set ``THEME = ec`` for a EC-themed UI.

The next step is to choose how to build and run the Angular UI application. Its resources are defined in
the ``gitb-ui/ui`` folder and its build is managed by Angular CLI. You have two options on how to work with
the Angular app - choose the preferred approach for you from

summary.text: Gives the development steps for gitb-ui: sbt compile, a run configuration for sbt run, and environment variables as needed (e.g. THEME = ec), then npm install in gitb-ui/ui before choosing one of two ways to work on the Angular app. When developing with EU Login, SESSION_SECURE must be false and SESSION_COOKIE_NAME ITB_SESSION, or session cookies are never served over HTTP and authentication loops; testing over HTTPS through a local SSL proxy is the alternative.

blocks.title: Option 1: Work on Angular UI through Play application
blocks.content:
### Option 1: Work on Angular UI through Play application

Using this approach you build the Angular app using Angular CLI but access it through the Play application. To do this:
1. From ``gitb-ui/ui`` issue ``npm run build``. This will build the app and copy it under the Play application's ``assets``
   folder. To rebuild automatically for any changes use ``npm run build:dev``.
2. Access the application by first going to the Play application's welcome page at http://localhost:9000. Once you click
   any of the login options the Angular app will be launched.
3. Once any part of the Angular app

summary.text: Describes the first way to develop the Angular UI: build it with npm run build (or npm run build:dev to rebuild on change) into the Play application's assets and reach it through the Play welcome page at localhost:9000, refreshing the browser after rebuilds. This mirrors production and is needed to test interactions with the Play application, such as EU Login and the various login options.

blocks.title: Option 2: Work on Angular UI standalone
blocks.content:
### Option 2: Work on Angular UI standalone 

Using this approach you build and serve the Angular app using Angular CLI. In this scenario the Play application
is only used through its REST API which the Angular app proxies and uses. To use this approach:
- Only once from ``gitb-ui/ui`` issue  ``npm run build``. This is needed to put in place static resources used by the Angular app
  (most notably tinymce styles).
- From ``gitb-ui/ui`` issue ``npm start``. This reloads the app upon detected changes.
- Access the application at http://localhost:4200 (this will be automatically opened for you).

summary.text: Describes the second way to develop the Angular UI: run npm run build once for static resources, then npm start to serve the app at localhost:4200 with automatic reload, using the Play application only through its proxied REST API. It is the most efficient approach but cannot test Play interactions such as EU Login, although it can be used after authenticating through Play since cookies are shared.

blocks.title: Build for deployment
blocks.content:
# Build for deployment

Follow these steps to build the components for deployment as a Dockerised service. Two approaches are available:
* [Build using the project's development tools](#build-using-development-tools).
* [Build using Docker Compose (containerised build)](#build-using-docker-compose).

summary.text: Heading that introduces building the components as a Dockerised service, by one of two approaches: with the project's development tools, or with Docker Compose as a containerised build.

blocks.title: Build using development tools
blocks.content:
## Build using development tools

This approach is more suitable is you have set up the repository for development and have [installed all necessary tooling](#prerequisites).
Producing build artefacts is faster but expects the necessary tools (Java, Maven, NPM, SBT, Scala) to be installed, and manual steps
to build Docker images.

summary.text: Says building with the development tools suits a repository already set up for development: it is faster but requires Java, Maven, NPM, SBT and Scala to be installed and the Docker images to be built by hand.

blocks.title: Test engine (gitb-srv)
blocks.content:
### Test engine (gitb-srv)

1. From the current (root) folder issue ``mvn clean install -DskipTests=true -Denv=docker``
2. Copy file ``gitb-testbed-service/target/itbsrv.war`` to a separate folder to build its Docker image.
3. Use Dockerfile ``etc/docker/gitb-srv/Dockerfile`` from the same folder to build the image with `docker build -t isaitb/gitb-srv .`.

summary.text: Gives the deployment build steps for gitb-srv: run mvn clean install -DskipTests=true -Denv=docker from the root, copy gitb-testbed-service/target/itbsrv.war to a separate folder, and build the isaitb/gitb-srv image there with the Dockerfile from etc/docker/gitb-srv.

blocks.title: Frontend (gitb-ui)
blocks.content:
### Frontend (gitb-ui)

1. From the ``gitb-ui`` folder issue ``sbt clean dist``. This builds all Play code and automatically calls the required
   prod build target from its Angular app.
2. Unzip the contents of the ``gitb-ui/target/universal/gitb-1.0-SNAPSHOT.zip`` archive to a separate folder. The name of the resulting unzipped folder should be ``gitb-ui``.
3. Use the Dockerfile ``etc/docker/gitb-ui/Dockerfile`` from the same folder to build the image with `docker build -t isaitb/gitb-ui .`.

summary.text: Gives the deployment build steps for gitb-ui: run sbt clean dist (which also runs the Angular production build), unzip gitb-ui/target/universal/gitb-1.0-SNAPSHOT.zip into a folder named gitb-ui, and build the isaitb/gitb-ui image there with the Dockerfile from etc/docker/gitb-ui.

blocks.title: Database (gitb-mysql)
blocks.content:
### Database (gitb-mysql)

1. From the `etc/docker/gitb-mysql` folder build the image with `docker build -t isaitb/gitb-mysql .`

summary.text: Gives the one step to build the database image: docker build -t isaitb/gitb-mysql from the etc/docker/gitb-mysql folder.

blocks.title: Session cache (gitb-redis)
blocks.content:
### Session cache (gitb-redis)

1. From the `etc/docker/gitb-redis` folder build the image with `docker build -t isaitb/gitb-redis .`

summary.text: Gives the one step to build the session-cache image: docker build -t isaitb/gitb-redis from the etc/docker/gitb-redis folder.

blocks.title: Create the overall service
blocks.content:
### Create the overall service

1. Follow the [development installation guide](https://www.itb.ec.europa.eu/docs/guides/latest/installingTheTestBed/index.html).
2. Create or [download](https://www.itb.ec.europa.eu/docs/guides/latest/_downloads/d863ccca4f45b40bb17be79b4841ad4b/docker-compose.yml) your docker-compose.yml file
   making use of the locally built images (see previous steps).
3. Launch the service from the folder containing your `docker-compose.yml` file with `docker compose up -d`.

summary.text: Explains how to assemble the service from locally built images: follow the development installation guide, create or download a docker-compose.yml that uses those images, and start it with docker compose up -d.

blocks.title: Build using Docker Compose
blocks.content:
## Build using Docker Compose

This approach is more suitable for a containerised build, avoiding any manual steps and developer tool installations (apart from Docker Compose). Make sure that your 
Docker Compose is at least at version `2.0.0`. Note that the overall build time in this case is slower compared to building with the relevant tools.

When using this approach the images are built directly from the repository's sources using the definitions in `docker-compose.yml`. As part of this process, select
configuration values are passed as Docker build arguments and embedded in the resulting

summary.text: Describes the containerised build with Docker Compose 2.0.0 or later, which builds all images from source with no developer tools but is slower. Six variables must be set first, and some are embedded in the images as build arguments: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD, MYSQL_PASSWORD, DB_DEFAULT_PASSWORD (which must match MYSQL_PASSWORD), APPLICATION_SECRET, MASTER_PASSWORD and HMAC_KEY (shared by gitb-ui and gitb-srv). It gives example settings for Linux/macOS and PowerShell or a .env file, then docker compose up -d --build. These images are for development, and the published images still support runtime secrets via environment variables and _FILE variants.

blocks.title: Using the application
blocks.content:
# Using the application

Once a complete Test Bed instance has been set up, either in development or as a Dockerised service, access using the default
Test Bed administrator account as follows:
1. Go to http://localhost:9000.
2. Click on the login button.
3. Authenticate using `admin@itb`. This account is set with a one-time password that is refreshed at start-up until a
   first login is made. The password to use is obtained by checking the logs of container `gitb-ui`.

An example log output to retrieve the administrator password is as follows: 
```
###########################################

summary.text: Explains first access to a running Test Bed: go to localhost:9000, click login and authenticate as admin@itb with a one-time password, refreshed at each start-up until the first login, that is printed in the gitb-ui container logs (an example log excerpt is shown). The user guide and sample tutorials cover what comes next.

For feedback or questions regarding the GITB Test Bed software you are invited to post issues in the current repository. In addition,
feel free to contact the Test Bed team via email at [DIGIT-ITB@ec.europa.eu](mailto:DIGIT-ITB@ec.europa.eu).

blocks.content:
# See also

For general information on all aspects of the Interoperability Test Bed and the GITB software in particular you may refer

The GITB software is used to realise a complete conformance testing platform. If you are more interested in standalone 
data validation you may find interesting the Test Bed's validators for [XML](https://github.com/ISAITB/xml-validator),
[RDF](https://github.com/ISAITB/shacl-validator), [JSON](

summary.text: Refers readers to the Interoperable Europe Portal site for general information on the Test Bed and GITB, and, for standalone data validation rather than a full conformance testing platform, to the Test Bed's separate XML, RDF (SHACL), JSON and CSV validators.
